desc:
Houses stand in a row and house i holds nums[i] coins. A plan is a set of house indices with no two neighbours (indices i and i + 1 never both in the plan); the empty plan is allowed. Two plans are different when their sets of indices differ, even if they collect the same coins.

Among all plans that collect the maximum possible number of coins, count how many there are. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007.

For example, for [1, 1, 1, 1] the maximum is 2 and there are 3 best plans (houses {0,2}, {0,3} and {1,3}), and for [0, 0, 0] every valid plan is best: there are 5 of them.
hints: First solve the usual question: the maximum total. Now ask the DP to also remember in how many ways each maximum can be reached.
Let (best, ways) describe the first i houses. Skipping house i-1 gives the pair for the first i-1 houses; robbing it gives (best[i-2] + nums[i-1], ways[i-2]).

Compare the two candidate pairs. If one total is larger, take that pair. If they are equal, the plans are disjoint (one contains the house, the other does not), so the counts add up. Reduce counts modulo 1,000,000,007 but compare totals exactly.
editorial: Extend the House Robber state to a pair (best, ways) for each prefix, starting from (0, 1) for the empty prefix (the single plan that robs nothing). For the prefix ending at house p there are two disjoint families of plans: those that skip p, described by the previous prefix, and those that rob p, described by the prefix two steps back with nums[p] added to the total.

Keep the larger total; when the totals tie, add the counts, because a plan that contains p can never equal a plan that does not. Ties are frequent when the array has zeros, since robbing an empty house changes nothing but still creates a different plan. The answer is the count of the full prefix, reduced modulo 1,000,000,007. Totals never exceed 10<sup>7</sup>, so they are compared exactly. Time O(n), space O(1).
